content: To properly wear a respirator, first position the bottom strap over your head and place it around your neck, ensuring it sits below your ears. Then, use the fingertips of both hands to adjust the metal nosepiece at the top of the respirator. Mold the nosepiece to the shape of your nose using two fingers from each hand. Avoid pinching the nosepiece with one hand, as this may compromise the respirator's effectiveness. To check the seal of the respirator, perform a positive seal check by exhaling sharply. If leakage is detected, adjust the position and tension of the straps and retest the seal until it is properly secured. For a negative seal check, inhale deeply. Facial hair can interfere with achieving a proper seal, reducing the efficiency of particulate respirators. Healthcare workers with facial structure abnormalities may also face challenges in obtaining a good seal and may require alternative respiratory protection methods. Respirators should be replaced if they become wet or dirty. Medical masks, which are flat or pleated and secured with straps, are recommended for use when caring for patients with droplet-transmitted infections or during activities that may generate splashes or sprays of blood, body fluids, secretions, or excretions. However, medical masks do not provide adequate respiratory protection against small-particle aerosols (droplet nuclei) and should not be used for airborne-transmitted diseases unless particulate respirators are unavailable. Medical masks are not designed to create a face seal, allowing potential leakage around the edges, which limits their effectiveness against droplet nuclei. They should be replaced if they become wet or dirty. The design of natural ventilation systems in healthcare facilities is critical for infection prevention and control. Properly designed ventilation systems can enhance airflow and reduce the risk of respiratory infection transmission. Cross ventilation, achieved by placing openings on opposite sides of a room, allows outdoor air to flow across the space. Each room requiring ventilation should have a separate stack to prevent cross-contamination. Other methods, such as atria ventilation, solar chimneys, and wind towers, can be integrated into building designs to improve natural ventilation. These precautions aim to minimize the spread of infections and prevent direct contact with blood, body fluids, secretions, and non-intact skin. Hand hygiene is a cornerstone of standard precautions and should be performed routinely using alcohol-based hand rubs or soap and water, depending on the level of soiling. Environmental cleaning and disinfection are critical for reducing the bioburden of pathogens on surfaces and breaking the chain of transmission. Cleaning must precede disinfection to remove organic matter, and disinfectants should be used according to manufacturer recommendations. Common hospital disinfectants include sodium hypochlorite (household bleach) and alcohol.
